source.value:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq 0$ or $s = 0.$

- If $s \neq 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s = 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

- For $s > 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is convergent

- For $s < 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

Evaluating our integral for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{2}{s},$ defined for $s > 0.$

source.question: e-21599
source.value:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = 
\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=e^{-2t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq -2$ or $s = -2.$

- If $s \neq -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-2-s}{e}^{(-2-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>-2, \\ \infty ,\, & s<-2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-2) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-(-2))t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s \leq -2$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s > -2$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s > -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Laplace transform of $f(t)=e^{-2t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s+2},$ defined for $s > -2.$

decisions.question: e-21602

source.question: e-21602
source.value:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)=e^{2\textrm i t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{2\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{2\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i \sin\theta
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)= \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i} -  \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i}\left[\lim_{a\to \infty}e^{ -sa}\cdot \left(\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)\right)  \right].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s < 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s < 0.$

- For $s = 0,$ we have simply $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s = 0.$

- For $s > 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $e^{2\textrm i t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i},$ defined for $s>0.$
